content_html_sanitized:
Posted April 25, 2002

Analysis by Richard Cowan

Two weeks ago NORML launched its $500,000

The first part was a large photo of a smiling Mayor Bloomberg with his now famous quote about having smoked cannabis: " You bet I did and I enjoyed it. " This part got national media coverage for days, especially on the nightly comedy shows with Letterman, Leno, et al.

However, the second part was the meat and that part wasn't funny:

" One in three adult Americans say they've smoked pot; 19 million in the last year. So why are we arresting people for doing something normal?

We don't arrest responsible drinkers. And it's well known that alcohol is much more harmful than marijuana. Yet 50,000 people a year are being arrested in New York City simply for smoking pot. Nearly 1,000 people a week. Many spend time in jail. Some get criminal records and lose college scholarships or jobs. A recent poll shows most New Yorkers are against such arrests. It's a waste of taxpayer money. And with heightened concern over terrorism, it's a foolish use of scarce law enforcement resources. There is an alternative. Private adult use of marijuana should be just that: a private matter. Those who light up in public can be issued a citation, as is currently done for public drinking, instead of being arrested and jailed. Is that a common sense policy? You bet it is. "

I think that this may be the first time that the city's marijuana arrest statistics have ever appeared in the New York Times. All the news that's fit to print? In fact, the only newspaper reports on the arrests that I have seen were in the tabloid, New York Daily News.
See

Recently, there was a bit of a flap when it was reported that ABC-TV was considering replacing its news program Nightline with David Letterman, if they could lure him away from CBS.

In " serious " circles -- the people who watch news programs -- that was blasphemy. The shock! The horror!

But someone unkindly pointed out that more Americans now learn about the news on the satirical monologues that begin Letterman and Leno, et al., than on the network news programs.

The sad fact is that if NORML had used the full page in The Times with the sort of sober and detailed arguments that The Times supposedly embodies, no one would have read it, and certainly it would not have been mentioned on the all important " news " segments of the satirists.

Indeed, the fact that hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers have been arrested for simple possession of cannabis in a supposedly tolerant city in a " decrim " state did not get talked about much, but thousands of people learned about NORML and its web site and have emailed them.

Newspapers and TV news programs across the country and around the world, including Paraguay and South Africa, called NORML and reported on the ads.

And speaking of exotic locations, there was one almost miraculous result: The Washington Post not only reported on the ad, and mentioned NORML, they actually reported the arrest numbers in an article on page 2 on Sunday, April 14, 2002:
" Bloomberg, 60, made it clear that what he might have found pleasant is nevertheless still illegal, and that arrests for possession and use of the weed will continue. More than 52,000 people were arrested for smoking pot last year, up from 720 in 1992. "
See

The Post never reports the national arrest numbers, although they do regularly report the arrest of athletes on marijuana charges. One would get the impression from The Post that only jocks smoke marijuana, and they tend to be a remarkably careless lot!
See

Buying a full-page ad in The Times is a part of the DEAland political ritual. It shows that your issue is at least a contender to be on the public agenda.

But if your issue is cannabis, after millions of Americans have been arrested, after millions more have suffered because it is a forbidden medicine, after we have lost so many of our individual rights in the decades old war on a plant, and after the economy and the environment have been greatly damaged by the suppression of hemp, we still have to lead with a laugh.

There is a book by media critic Neil Postman, Amusing Ourselves to Death. As the title indicates, we have turned news reporting into a form of entertainment and that is undermining democracy. The good and bad news is that we have also turned entertainment into a form of reporting. Now if we could just learn something that isn't funny.
